c.tagline: Golden Ring jewel where the Volga meets the Kotorosl.

taxi.fareNote: Use Yandex Go for reliable metered fares; hailed street taxis may not run the meter, so agree a price first.

emergency.note: 112 is the unified emergency number that connects to police, ambulance and fire.

hood_landmark.Korovniki: Church of John Chrysostom, Korovniki, Yaroslavl
hood_landmark.Krasny Perekop (Tolchkovo): Church of John the Baptist, Yaroslavl

avoid.reason: Give drunken groups near the train station and riverside parks a wide berth late at night; otherwise usual city awareness.

hood_desc: The UNESCO-listed historic core around Sovetskaya Square, with the Volkov Theatre, Spassky (Transfiguration) Monastery, the Church of Elijah the Prophet, shops and cafes all walkable; the natural base for first-timers.
The cape at the confluence of the Volga and Kotorosl rivers, with the landscaped Strelka Park, the Assumption Cathedral and a long riverside promenade; scenic and central for sightseeing on foot.

A quieter riverside quarter across the Kotorosl famous for its 17th-century church ensemble (Church of John Chrysostom and the leaning Korovniki bell tower); atmospheric and historic, away from the bustle.
The left bank of the Volga, a greener, mostly residential district reached by bridge, home to the 14th-century Tolga Convent; calm and local, good for a slower pace.
A traditional textile district south of the centre, best known for the elaborate Church of St John the Baptist in Tolchkovo (the church pictured on the 1000-ruble note); low-key and residential.

water.note: Tap water is treated but locals typically boil or filter it; bottled is safest.

transit.hours: Trams, trolleybuses and buses generally run from about 5:30 AM to 11:00 PM; marshrutka minibuses and taxis fill late-night gaps.
transit.note: Yaroslavl has one of Russia's oldest tram networks plus trolleybuses, city buses and marshrutka minibuses; there is no metro.
transit.pay: Pay the driver or conductor in cash or by contactless bank card on board (around 28-35 rubles per ride); a local transport card gives small discounts.

bus: Yaroslavl Central Bus Station — intercity coaches to Moscow, Kostroma, Vologda and Rybinsk
ferry: Volga River passenger boats & cruise piers (seasonal, summer)
train: Yaroslavl-Glavny & Yaroslavl-Moskovsky stations — Northern Railway, ~3.5-4 h to Moscow

transit.m: Shuttle bus / marshrutka to city centre (~30-40 min)

tip.r: Not obligatory; rounding up the bill or leaving 5-10% for good restaurant service is appreciated but not expected.

food.name: Ukha (Volga fish soup)
food.desc: Clear golden broth of river fish - zander, pike, sometimes sterlet - with potato and dill. Yaroslavl sits on the Volga and cooks accordingly.

places.name: Sobranie
places.note: Russian-cuisine restaurant built around Volga river fish; its fish dishes are the draw.

places.name: Burlak
places.note: Volga-themed dining room right on the river promenade, strong on freshwater fish.

places.name: Ioann Vasilyevich
places.note: Yaroslavl's best-known themed restaurant; hearty old-Russian cooking and heavy bookings.

food.name: Yarushki (Volga fish dumplings)
food.desc: Small hand-pinched dumplings stuffed with Volga zander and pike, served in a rich fish broth - a Yaroslavl speciality you will not find elsewhere.

places.name: Sobranie
places.note: The house signature: yarushki rybolepnye, fish dumplings in their own broth.

places.name: Burlak
places.note: River-fish menu with dumplings and pies made from the day's catch.

places.name: Ioann Vasilyevich
places.note: Does the fish and meat dumpling classics in generous old-fashioned portions.

food.name: Baked sudak (zander)
food.desc: Volga pike-perch baked in sour cream with mushrooms and onion until the top browns - the classic upper-Volga way with the river's best-eating fish.

places.name: Burlak
places.note: Embankment restaurant whose whole point is Volga fish, cooked simply.

places.name: Sobranie
places.note: Careful Russian cooking with a serious fish section on the menu.

places.name: Penaty
places.note: Long-standing Russian restaurant popular with locals for fish mains and set lunches.

food.name: Pelmeni
food.desc: Thin-skinned meat dumplings boiled and served with butter, sour cream and vinegar or black pepper - Russia's default comfort food, made by hand here.

places.name: Ioann Vasilyevich
places.note: Big plates of hand-made pelmeni in a theatrically old-Russian dining room.

places.name: Penaty
places.note: Reliable, unfussy Russian cooking at prices locals actually pay.

places.name: Sobranie
places.note: Makes several dumpling varieties, including the fish yarushki.

food.name: Rasstegai and pirogi
food.desc: Open-topped fish pies and closed pastries filled with cabbage, mushroom, egg or berries, sold by the piece from bakeries and eaten with soup.

places.name: Yaroslavl Central Market bakeries
places.note: Bakery counters inside the market turn out pirogi and rasstegai all morning.

places.name: Volzhskaya Embankment trakteers
places.note: Old-style taverns along the river bake their own pies and serve them with tea.

places.name: Ioann Vasilyevich
places.note: Serves rasstegai alongside the ukha, which is how they are meant to be eaten.

food.name: Blini
food.desc: Thin buckwheat or wheat pancakes rolled around sour cream, salted fish, mushrooms or jam - the everyday version of Russia's oldest food.

places.name: Volzhskaya Embankment trakteers
places.note: Riverside taverns with their own baking, terraces open through the summer.

places.name: Penaty
places.note: Blini with caviar or mushrooms as a starter before the heavier Russian mains.

places.name: Yaroslavl Central Market food row
places.note: Cheap fresh blini griddled to order among the produce stalls.

food.name: Medovukha
food.desc: Honey ale brewed from fermented honey with herbs and spices - lightly alcoholic, faintly sweet and served in earthenware mugs, warm in winter.

places.name: Ioann Vasilyevich
places.note: Serves medovukha and sbiten in keeping with its old-Russian theme.

places.name: Volzhskaya Embankment trakteers
places.note: Riverside taverns keep several honey brews on the drinks list.

places.name: Yaroslavl Central Market
places.note: Bottled medovukha and honey from regional producers sold at the honey stalls.

food.name: Mors
food.desc: Cold berry cordial pressed from cranberries, lingonberries or sea buckthorn and lightly sweetened - tart, non-alcoholic and on every Russian menu.

places.name: Penaty
places.note: House-made mors by the jug, the standard accompaniment to a Russian lunch.

places.name: Sobranie
places.note: Makes its own berry morsy from northern fruit alongside the kvass.

places.name: Yaroslavl Central Market
places.note: Berry sellers bottle their own mors, cheapest and freshest in the city.

landmarks: Transfiguration Monastery (Spaso-Preobrazhensky)
A white-walled fortress-monastery where Russia's epic 'Tale of Igor's Campaign' was discovered; climb its belfry for views over golden domes.
Church of Elijah the Prophet
The 17th-century jewel of Yaroslavl's UNESCO-listed center, its interior ablaze with some of Russia's finest preserved frescoes.
Volga Embankment
A genteel tree-lined promenade above the great river, strung with gazebos, museums and merchant mansions—perfect for a slow evening stroll.
Strelka Park
The arrow-shaped spit where the Kotorosl meets the Volga, site of the city's 1010 founding, now landscaped with fountains and monuments.
Assumption Cathedral
Rebuilt for the city's millennium in 2010 with gleaming golden domes, the cathedral once again commands the skyline above the Strelka.
Church of St. John the Baptist at Tolchkovo
A fifteen-domed brick masterpiece pictured on Russia's 1,000-ruble note, containing one of the largest fresco cycles in the Orthodox world.
Volkov Drama Theatre
Founded in 1750 as Russia's first professional public theatre, it still stages acclaimed performances behind a handsome neoclassical facade.
Chapel of Our Lady of Kazan
The rocket-shaped 1997 chapel beside the monastery honors the 1612 volunteer army and also stars on the 1,000-ruble banknote.
Yaroslavl Art Museum (Governor's House)
An elegant riverside governor's mansion turned gallery of icons and 19th-century Russian painting, set in a sculpture-dotted garden.
Church of the Epiphany
A red-brick 17th-century church encrusted with glazed tiles, its slender green domes a textbook example of the Yaroslavl architectural style.

train.note: No international trains. Yaroslavl-Glavny is on the northern main line with Lastochka fast trains to Moscow Yaroslavsky in about 3 hours and long-distance services continuing north to Vologda and Arkhangelsk and east on the Trans-Siberian route. Foreign cards often fail on the RZD site.

bus.note: No international coaches. The bus station south of the centre runs services to Kostroma, Rostov Veliky, Uglich and Moscow. Tickets are sold at the terminal; the train is faster and more comfortable for Moscow.

intl.to: Volga river towns - Tolga & Konstantinovo (Russia) - seasonal, May-Oct
intl.op: Yaroslavl river passenger fleet — tickets at the river terminal

ferry.note: There are no sea ferries - Yaroslavl is inland on the Volga. Seasonal river boats from the terminal serve nearby settlements and the Tolga monastery, and the city is a standard stop on the multi-day Moscow-St Petersburg Volga cruises. Everything stops when the river freezes, roughly November to April.

half.name: Rostov Veliky
half.blurb: Golden Ring town on Lake Nero with a walled kremlin of onion-domed churches.

half.name: Tutayev
half.blurb: Volga riverside town split into two halves by the river, with old churches on each bank.

full.name: Kostroma
full.blurb: Golden Ring city on the Volga known for the fortified Ipatiev Monastery and its historic fire-lookout tower.

full.name: Pereslavl-Zalessky
full.blurb: Lakeside town with several working monasteries and the birthplace site of Peter the Great's first navy.
